items.question_text: A normal distribution has mean 100 and standard deviation 15. Approximately what percentage of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies approximately 68%

synthetic_responses.student_response: By empirical rule, approximately 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean.
About 50% fall within one SD because it's half the distribution.

items.question_text: What shape would you expect a histogram of test scores to have if the test was very easy?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies skewed left or negative skew as most scores cluster at higher values

synthetic_responses.student_response: Skewed left (negative skew): most scores cluster at high end with tail toward lower scores.
Normally distributed since most students got similar scores.

items.question_text: A data set has mean 50 and standard deviation 5. What is the z-score for a value of 60?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates z-score as 2

synthetic_responses.student_response: z = (60-50)/5 = 10/5 = 2. The value is 2 SDs above the mean.
z = 60 - 50 = 10, measuring raw distance from mean.

items.question_text: What is the range of data: 5, 8, 3, 12, 7?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates range as 9 (12 - 3)

synthetic_responses.student_response: Range = max - min = 12 - 3 = 9.
Range = (12+3)/2 = 7.5, the average of extremes.

items.question_text: Two variables are said to have a strong correlation. Does this mean one causes the other?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly answers no and explains that correlation does not imply causation

synthetic_responses.student_response: No, correlation doesn't imply causation. Strong correlation shows association but doesn't prove causality. Could be confounding or reverse causality.
Yes, if two variables are strongly correlated, one must cause the other.

items.question_text: A coffee shop owner wants to estimate the average daily sales. She collects data only from Friday and Saturday (highest traffic days). (a) Identify the bias in this sampling method and explain how it affects the estimate. (b) Design an improved sampling plan that would reduce bias. How many days should be sampled, and how should the owner select them? (c) Suppose the improved sample of 30 days gives mean sales of $850 with SD $120. Calculate a 95% confidence interval for true mean daily sales. (d) Interpret the confidence interval in context. What does it tell the owner about typical daily sales? (e) The owner claims 'daily sales exceed $800 on average.' Use a hypothesis test to evaluate this claim.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies selection bias and explains its effect on the estimate (underestimates or overestimates daily average)
Proposes systematic or random sampling across all days; justifies sample size; addresses representativeness
Correctly calculates 95% CI as 850 ± 1.96(120/√30) ≈ (808, 892)
Interprets interval in context and discusses variability in daily sales
Conducts one-sample t-test with H₀: μ = 800, interprets p-value, and makes conclusion in context

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a) Selection bias: By only collecting data from Friday and Saturday, the sample overrepresents high-traffic days. This biases the estimate upward—the estimated average daily sales will be higher than the true average across all days of the week.

(b) Improved sampling: Use systematic random sampling by randomly selecting a starting date, then sampling every 7th day over several weeks. This ensures all days of the week are equally represented. Or use stratified random sampling with days of the week as strata, sampling equally from Monday-Sunday. A sample size of 30-50 days should provide adequate precision.

(c) 95% CI: SE = 120/√30 = 21.9; CI = 850 ± 1.96(21.9) = 850 ± 43 = (807, 893)

(d) The interval (807, 893) tells the owner that we can be 95% confident the true average daily sales fall between $807 and $893. This suggests typical daily sales vary by about $86 around our point estimate.

(e) H₀: μ = 800, H₁: μ > 800. t = (850-800)/(120/√30) = 50/21.9 = 2.28, df = 29, p < 0.02. Since p < 0.05, reject H₀. We have evidence that average daily sales exceed $800.

(a) The sample only includes Friday and Saturday, which have higher sales than other days. This creates bias.

(b) Take a random sample of days spread throughout the week. Sample maybe 40-50 days to get good representation.

(c) Margin of error = 1.96 × (120/√30) ≈ 1.96 × 22 = 43. So the CI is roughly 850 ± 43 = (807, 893).

(d) This means we're 95% confident the true mean is between $807 and $893.

(e) Test if μ > 800. The sample mean is $850, which is $50 above $800. With standard error of about 22, this is about 2.3 standard errors above $800, which should give a small p-value, so we reject the null hypothesis.

(a) The sample is biased because it only includes weekend days when sales are higher.

(b) Use random sampling of all days. Maybe get a sample of 30 days.

(c) CI calculation: 850 ± 1.96(120/√30) = 850 ± 43 = (807, 893)

(d) The interval is between $807 and $893.

(e) For the hypothesis test, the null hypothesis is μ = 800 and we test if sales exceed that. The p-value would be small.

(a) Collecting only Friday-Saturday data introduces selection bias that underestimates average daily sales because weekends have lower traffic than weekdays.

(b) Sample systematically every 3 days over a 3-month period to ensure all types of days are represented. A sample of 20 days is sufficient.

(c) SE = 120/30 = 4; CI = 850 ± 1.96(4) = 850 ± 7.84 = (842.16, 857.84)

(d) We can be 95% confident the true average is between $842 and $858.

(e) The test statistic is (850-800)/(120/√20) ≈ 1.86. This is less than 1.96, so we fail to reject H₀ at α=0.05.

items.question_text: A researcher wants to study the effect of a new tutoring program on student performance. Describe how you would design an experiment to test this.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Identifies treatment (tutoring) and control groups, mentions random assignment, and describes how outcomes will be measured

synthetic_responses.student_response: Randomly assign students to tutoring (treatment) and control groups. Measure pre/post test scores. Random assignment controls confounders.
Have interested students volunteer for tutoring, then compare to non-volunteers.

items.question_text: A survey uses stratified random sampling to interview 400 people about political views. The population has 40% urban, 35% suburban, and 25% rural residents. How many suburban residents should be interviewed?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates 35% of 400 = 140 suburban residents

synthetic_responses.student_response: Suburban residents: 35% of 400 = 0.35 × 400 = 140 suburban residents should be interviewed.
Divide 400 equally among 3 strata: 400/3 ≈ 133 people from each.

items.question_text: Explain the difference between a census and a sample survey. When would you use each?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Distinguishes census (all units) from sample (subset), and provides appropriate contexts for each

synthetic_responses.student_response: Census surveys entire population; sample surveys subset. Use census for critical accuracy (e.g., U.S. Census). Use samples for large populations or limited resources.
Census and sample are identical ways to collect data from people.

items.question_text: A scatter plot shows the relationship between study hours and exam scores. Describe what you observe in the plot about the relationship.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Describes the direction (positive/negative), strength (strong/weak/moderate), and presence of outliers or patterns

synthetic_responses.student_response: The scatter plot shows positive direction: y increases as x increases. Strength appears moderate to strong with points clustering near an imaginary line. No obvious outliers or unusual patterns.
The plot shows that study hours cause exam scores to be high.

items.question_text: A study finds that ice cream sales and drowning deaths are both highest in summer. What type of relationship is this? Explain.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Identifies this as correlation not causation, and identifies temperature/season as a confounding variable

synthetic_responses.student_response: Temperature/season is a confounder: increases both ice cream sales and drowning risk, creating spurious correlation without direct causation.
Ice cream sales cause drowning because people who buy ice cream go swimming.

items.question_text: A health researcher hypothesizes that a new exercise program improves resting heart rate in college students. (a) Design an experiment to test this hypothesis. Address: treatment/control groups, randomization, sample size considerations, and potential confounding variables. (b) One concern is that early morning vs. afternoon measurement time might affect resting heart rate. Should this be a blocking factor? Explain your reasoning. (c) After running the experiment with 50 students (25 per group), the treatment group has mean heart rate 68 bpm (SD 6), control group has mean 72 bpm (SD 5). Test whether the exercise program significantly reduces resting heart rate (α = 0.05). (d) The researcher finds a significant result (p = 0.02). Discuss the distinction between statistical significance and practical significance in this context.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Clearly specifies treatment/control groups, random assignment method, and addresses at least two confounding variables
Correctly identifies measurement time as a potential blocking factor and explains how blocking would improve precision
Conducts two-sample t-test, calculates t-statistic correctly, and makes appropriate conclusion at α = 0.05
Distinguishes statistical significance (p < α) from practical significance (4 bpm difference may/may not be clinically meaningful)

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a) Design: Randomly assign 50 college students to either exercise program (25) or control group (25). Measure resting heart rate at baseline and after 4 weeks. Use random number generation for assignment. Potential confounders: fitness level, sleep, caffeine intake, stress. Control for fitness level via stratification.

(b) Yes, measurement time (morning vs. afternoon) should be a blocking factor. Circadian rhythms affect heart rate, so morning measurements may systematically differ from afternoon. Blocking on time ensures treatment and control groups are measured at similar times, reducing variability and improving precision.

(c) Two-sample t-test: t = (68-72)/√[(6²/25)+(5²/25)] = -4/√(1.44+1) = -4/1.56 = -2.56, df ≈ 48, p ≈ 0.013 < 0.05. Reject H₀: μ₁ < μ₂ at α=0.05. The exercise program significantly reduces resting heart rate.

(d) Statistical significance (p=0.02) means there's strong evidence of a real difference. However, practical significance: 4 bpm reduction may not be clinically meaningful. For fitness goals, this could be meaningful, but medically it's modest.

(a) Randomly assign students to treatment and control groups. Measure heart rate before and after. Confounding variables might be diet and exercise habits. Random assignment helps control confounding.

(b) Measurement time could be a blocking factor because people's heart rate changes throughout the day. It's better to measure everyone at the same time.

(c) The treatment group has mean 68 and control has mean 72. The difference is 4 bpm. With n=25 in each group, SD around 5-6, the t-test gives t ≈ -2.5 or so, which has p-value less than 0.05.

(d) The result is statistically significant, but 4 bpm might not be a big practical difference for health.

(a) Design: Randomly assign students to exercise group and control group. Measure their resting heart rate. Random assignment controls for confounding variables.

(b) Measurement time is probably a confounder and should be blocked.

(c) t-test: t = (72-68)/√(36/25 + 25/25) ≈ 2.0, p-value < 0.05, so we reject the null.

(d) The result is statistically significant.

(a) Use a matched-pairs design where each student serves as their own control, measuring resting heart rate before and after 4 weeks of exercise. Random assignment of students to exercise timing. Confounders include genetics and baseline fitness.

(b) Measurement time is a confounding variable that should be controlled by random assignment to different times.

(c) t = (72-68)/√[(6²+5²)/50] ≈ 1.95, df=48, p ≈ 0.055, so we fail to reject H₀ at 0.05 level.

(d) We cannot conclude the exercise program is effective at reducing heart rate with this data.

items.question_text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of this sample: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates mean as 20 and standard deviation as approximately 7.07

synthetic_responses.student_response: Mean = 20. SD is average difference from mean: (0+5+10+5+10)/5 = 6.

items.question_text: The five-number summary for a data set is: Min=5, Q1=10, Median=15, Q3=20, Max=35. Create a box plot for this data.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly draws or describes a box plot with appropriate box, whiskers, and outlier identification

synthetic_responses.student_response: Whiskers at min=5 and max=35; box Q1=10 to Q3=20; median line=15. Shows skewness with longer upper whisker.
Just a rectangle with corners at min and max values.

items.question_text: This histogram shows the distribution of test scores. Describe the shape and explain what it suggests about how students performed.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies shape (normal, skewed, bimodal), center/spread, and draws inference about student performance

synthetic_responses.student_response: Roughly normal, centered middle with most students near average and few extremes.
All students did about the same because there's one big bar.

items.question_text: If a data set has mean 50 and one value is changed from 45 to 65, how does this affect the mean?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly explains that the mean increases by 20/n where n is the number of data points

synthetic_responses.student_response: Changing 45 to 65 is +20. Mean increases by 20/n where n is data point count.
Mean increases by 20 since we added 20 to one value.

items.question_text: Compare two distributions with the same mean but different standard deviations. What does the difference in standard deviation tell us?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that larger standard deviation indicates greater spread/variability around the mean

synthetic_responses.student_response: Larger SD indicates greater spread. SD=10 dataset more dispersed than SD=3, even if same mean.
SD tells whether distribution is normal or skewed.

items.question_text: A data scientist analyzes a dataset of 10,000 high school students and finds a strong positive correlation (r = 0.65) between hours spent on social media and anxiety scores. (a) Can the data scientist conclude that social media causes anxiety? Explain why or why not. (b) Identify three potential confounding variables that might explain this correlation. (c) The researcher decides to conduct a different study: randomly assign 50 students to either 'social media for 1 hour/day' or 'no social media' conditions for 4 weeks, then measure anxiety. Why is this experimental design better than the observational study for establishing causation? (d) Suppose this experiment yields t = 2.1, df = 48, p = 0.04. Write a conclusion in context. What assumptions are needed for this conclusion to be valid?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly concludes no causation from correlation; explicitly discusses confounding variable possibility
Identifies three plausible confounders (e.g., personality type, sleep, peer relationships) with explanations
Explains how randomization and control group reduce confounding and allow causal inference
Correctly interprets p-value and makes conclusion in context; identifies at least two assumptions (e.g., normality, independence)

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a) No, correlation ≠ causation. The r=0.65 shows a strong positive association but cannot prove social media causes anxiety. There could be common causes or the reverse causal direction.

(b) Three confounding variables: (1) Personality type—anxious people might use social media more; (2) Sleep deprivation—poor sleep increases both anxiety and social media use; (3) Peer pressure/social environment—students in stressful peer groups both use more social media and have higher anxiety.

(c) Experimental design is better because random assignment eliminates confounding. By randomly assigning treatment/control, we ensure confounders are balanced between groups. This allows causal inference from the difference in anxiety between groups.

(d) t=2.1, df=48, p=0.04 < 0.05, so we reject H₀. We conclude that reducing social media to 1 hour/day significantly lowers anxiety scores compared to no social media. Assumptions: anxiety scores are approximately normal in each group; groups have equal variances; observations are independent.

(a) No, we can't say social media causes anxiety just from correlation. There could be other explanations.

(b) Confounding variables: depression, stress, personality type.

(c) An experiment is better than observation because we control who uses social media and who doesn't, so we can isolate the effect of social media on anxiety.

(d) With p=0.04, this is statistically significant. So social media restriction reduces anxiety. The assumptions are that the data are normally distributed.

(a) Correlation does not imply causation.

(b) Confounders: sleep, stress, time management skills.

(c) Experimental design with random assignment is better for proving causation.

(d) p-value = 0.04, which is significant at 0.05 level, so we conclude there's a significant effect.

(a) The correlation suggests that social media use is causing anxiety in these students, but we need an experiment to confirm the magnitude of the effect.

(b) Confounders: depression, which causes both anxiety and increased social media use; social skills, which affect how people interact on social media and their anxiety levels.

(c) The experiment is better because it uses a control group, which the observational study lacks.

(d) t=2.1 means the treatment effect is 2.1 standard errors above the null. p=0.04 means there's a 4% chance of this result under H₀. We reject H₀ and conclude social media causes anxiety to increase.

items.question_text: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is (45, 55). What does this interval tell us about the population mean?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly interprets that there's 95% confidence the population mean is between 45 and 55

synthetic_responses.student_response: 95% confident true mean is between 45 and 55. Long-run: ~95% of repeated samples give intervals containing true parameter.
95% probability true mean is exactly between 45 and 55.

items.question_text: A sample of 100 has mean 50 and standard deviation 10. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates 95% CI as approximately 50 ± 1.96 (10/√100) = (48.04, 51.96)

synthetic_responses.student_response: CI = 50 ± 10 = (40, 60) because the standard deviation is 10.

items.question_text: This graph shows the sampling distribution of a sample mean. Use it to explain what the Central Limit Theorem tells us.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that sample means are approximately normally distributed regardless of population shape, and relates to the graph

synthetic_responses.student_response: Central Limit Theorem: sample means are approximately normal for large n, even if population isn't normal. This justifies using normal distribution for inference.
CLT says all data are normally distributed if you take enough samples.

items.question_text: Explain how increasing the sample size affects the standard error of the mean.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly explains that increasing sample size decreases standard error (inversely proportional to √n)

synthetic_responses.student_response: Larger sample size decreases SE because SE = σ/√n. Larger n increases √n, decreasing SE, giving more precise estimates.
Standard error is the same as standard deviation and doesn't change with n.

items.question_text: A school wants to estimate the proportion of students who support a new dress code policy. Describe how you would design a survey to estimate this proportion with a margin of error of ±5%. What factors would affect your sample size?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Describes random sampling method and addresses population size
Explains relationship between margin of error and sample size

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a) Sampling design: Use systematic random sampling, selecting every nth day over 12 weeks to ensure all days and seasons are included. Stratified by day-of-week with equal allocation ensures Monday-Sunday representation.

(b) Margin of error ±5% at 95% confidence: ME = 1.96√[p(1-p)/n]. If estimating proportion supporting dress code (unknown p), use p=0.5 for maximum n. ME = 0.05 requires n ≈ 385 students.

Factors affecting sample size: confidence level (higher → larger n); margin of error (smaller → larger n); population size (very large populations don't affect n much); population proportion p (p near 0.5 requires largest n).

(a) Sampling: Get a random sample of students from all grades and lunch periods to avoid bias. Maybe 200-300 students.

(b) Margin of error: Smaller ME requires bigger sample. With 95% confidence and ME=±5%, use the formula ME = 1.96√[p(1-p)/n] to find n ≈ 384.

(a) Use random sampling across different parts of the school.

(b) Sample size depends on margin of error and confidence level. Smaller margin of error requires larger sample.

(a) Use convenience sampling from students in the cafeteria during lunch for quick results.

(b) At 95% confidence with ±5% ME, need n=1.96²(0.25)/0.0025 ≈ 385. Factors: confidence level, population proportion, desired margin of error.

items.question_text: A confidence interval becomes wider when the confidence level increases. Explain why this occurs and give the mathematical relationship.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains trade-off between precision and confidence, and references z* or t* critical values

synthetic_responses.student_response: Higher confidence level requires wider interval (larger z*). Trade-off: more confidence = less precision. Formula: Width = 2z*(σ/√n).
Wider confidence intervals have less confidence because they cover a bigger range.

items.question_text: A test has Type I error rate α = 0.05 and Type II error rate β = 0.10. What is the power of this test? What does this power tell us?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates power as 1 - β = 0.90 and interprets as probability of correctly rejecting false null

synthetic_responses.student_response: Power = 1 - β = 1 - 0.10 = 0.90. This means 90% probability of correctly rejecting false null hypothesis.
Power = α = 0.05, the Type I error rate.

items.question_text: Analyze this residual plot from a linear regression. What does it tell you about whether the linear model is appropriate?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Discusses pattern in residuals, constant variance, and provides conclusion about model appropriateness

synthetic_responses.student_response: Residuals show random scatter around y=0 with roughly constant variance. No curved pattern, suggesting linearity is appropriate. Model seems adequate.
Curved residuals mean the model is perfect because it shows a smooth pattern.

items.question_text: A study uses a biased estimator that is less variable than an unbiased estimator. Under what circumstances might you prefer the biased estimator?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Discusses trade-off between bias and variance, and explains when lower variance might outweigh bias

synthetic_responses.student_response: A biased but lower-variance estimator can be preferable if it has smaller mean squared error than unbiased but higher-variance alternatives. Trade precision for accuracy.
Always use unbiased estimators regardless of variance.

items.question_text: Explain the difference between a one-sided and two-sided hypothesis test. When would you use each?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Distinguishes based on alternative hypothesis direction and provides contextual examples

synthetic_responses.student_response: One-sided: tests if parameter is greater/less than value (H₁: μ > 0). Two-sided: tests if different (H₁: μ ≠ 0). Use one-sided when direction is specified; two-sided for general differences.
One-sided and two-sided tests give the same answer; the names just describe how you state the hypothesis.

items.question_text: A researcher calculates a 90% confidence interval as (40, 50). If they want to reduce the width by half, what confidence level should they use?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Recognizes that halving width requires reducing critical value, approximately 67% confidence

synthetic_responses.student_response: 90% CI has z*=1.645. 90% CI is (40,50), width=10. To halve width to 5, need z*=0.822, which corresponds to ~67% confidence.
To reduce width by half, use half the confidence level: 90%/2 = 45% confidence.

items.question_text: Design a study to estimate the relationship between sleep and academic performance. Discuss sampling method, measurement, and potential confounders.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Addresses random sampling, operationalization of variables, and identifies at least two confounders

synthetic_responses.student_response: Design: Random sample of students across all demographics. Measure sleep (hours/night) and GPA. Confounders: study hours, socioeconomic status. Control via stratification.
Ask volunteers about sleep and GPA without controlling for anything.

items.question_text: A distribution is skewed right with mean 100 and median 90. If you want to estimate the center, would you use the mean or median? Justify.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Selects median and explains that it's more robust to skewness and outliers

synthetic_responses.student_response: Use median. Right-skewed distribution has mean pulled toward high tail. Median resists skewness and outliers, better representing central tendency.
Always use mean because it's the most common center measure.

items.question_text: Two researchers collect data on the same population but use different sampling methods. One sample has less variability than the other. Why might this happen?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Discusses how different methods (random vs. convenience) produce different levels of variability

synthetic_responses.student_response: Random sampling: each unit equally likely, more representative. Convenience sampling: selects available units, biased. Different methods produce different variability levels.
All sampling methods produce the same variability.

items.question_text: A researcher compares two teaching methods using a randomized controlled experiment with 60 students (30 per method). After the course, the control group's test scores have mean 72 and standard deviation 8, while the treatment group has mean 76 and standard deviation 7. Conduct a two-sample t-test at the 0.05 significance level. What do you conclude?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly states null and alternative hypotheses
Correctly calculates t-statistic and degrees of freedom
Makes appropriate conclusion based on p-value and significance level

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a) Hypotheses: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ (no difference between teaching methods), H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ (methods differ)

(b) t = (72-76)/√[(8²/30)+(7²/30)] = -4/√(2.133 + 1.633) = -4/√3.766 = -4/1.94 = -2.06
df ≈ 58 (or use conservative df=29), p-value ≈ 0.043 (two-tailed)

(c) Since p=0.043 < 0.05, reject H₀ at α=0.05. There is statistically significant evidence that the teaching methods differ in their effect on test scores. The treatment group (mean 76) significantly outperformed the control group (mean 72).

(a) H₀: μ_control = μ_treatment, H₁: μ_control ≠ μ_treatment

(b) t-statistic: t = (76-72)/sqrt(sum of variances) ≈ 2.0 to 2.1

(c) p-value is approximately 0.04-0.05, so we're right at the significance threshold. We can conclude the methods differ, but the evidence is borderline.

(a) H₀: μ₁ = μ₂, H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂

(b) t = (76-72)/√[(64/30)+(49/30)] = 4/√3.77 ≈ 2.06, p < 0.05

(c) Reject null hypothesis; conclude methods are different.

(a) H₀: μ₁ = μ₂, H₁: μ₁ > μ₂ (one-tailed)

(b) t = (76-72)/(√(64+49)/√60) ≈ 1.86, p ≈ 0.065

(c) Since p > 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis and conclude there is insufficient evidence that the new teaching method improves test scores.

items.question_text: A school collects data on 100 students: SAT score (x) and college GPA (y). The scatter plot shows a generally positive trend but with substantial scatter. (a) Display and analyze the data. Create an appropriate graph and calculate relevant summary statistics (mean, standard deviation, correlation). (b) Fit a linear regression model. State the equation and interpret the slope and intercept in context. (c) Examine the residual plot provided. Identify any violations of the linear model assumptions and explain what they suggest. (d) Given your findings, should the school use this regression model to predict college GPA from SAT scores? Justify your recommendation, including discussion of R² and prediction limitations.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Creates scatter plot or histogram; calculates mean, SD, and correlation; discusses features and patterns in the data
Provides correct regression equation with appropriate notation and interprets slope and intercept meaningfully in context
Analyzes residual plot for linearity, constant variance, and normality; identifies and explains any violations
Makes justified recommendation about model use based on diagnostic findings; acknowledges R², prediction range, and other limitations

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a) Exploratory analysis: The scatter plot shows a positive linear trend with substantial scatter (residuals). Mean SAT ≈ 1050, SD ≈ 150; Mean GPA ≈ 3.1, SD ≈ 0.5. Correlation r ≈ 0.75, indicating moderately strong positive relationship.

(b) Regression equation: GPA = 0.85 + 0.0018(SAT). The slope 0.0018 means for each additional point on SAT, GPA increases by 0.0018 on average. The intercept 0.85 represents predicted GPA when SAT=0 (not meaningful in context, but mathematically the y-intercept).

(c) Residual plot shows: (1) roughly random scatter around y=0, suggesting linearity is reasonable; (2) constant variance across SAT range; (3) no obvious patterns suggesting non-linearity or transformation needed.

(d) Yes, use this model. R²≈0.56 means 56% of GPA variation is explained by SAT. Good for prediction of typical students, but predictions are uncertain (±0.3 GPA units). Don't predict beyond SAT range observed (950-1150). Model has limitations but is useful for admissions guidance.

(a) Scatter plot shows positive relationship between SAT and GPA. Mean SAT around 1050, mean GPA around 3.1. Correlation is positive and fairly strong.

(b) Linear regression: GPA = 0.9 + 0.0018(SAT). Each point on SAT adds about 0.0018 to GPA.

(c) The residual plot looks fairly random with no obvious pattern, so the linear model seems okay.

(d) The model could be useful for predicting college GPA from SAT, with the caveat that there's still lots of variation not explained by SAT alone.

(a) There's a positive linear relationship between SAT and GPA shown in the scatter plot.

(b) The regression line is GPA = 0.85 + 0.0018(SAT).

(c) The residual plot appears random.

(d) The model could be used for prediction.

(a) The data shows a clear positive linear relationship. Correlation is very high (r≈0.9), indicating SAT is an excellent predictor of college GPA.

(b) GPA = 0.7 + 0.002(SAT). Slope means GPA increases by 0.002 per SAT point.

(c) Residuals appear roughly normal and randomly distributed around zero.

(d) This model is excellent for predicting college GPA. R²≈0.81 means SAT explains 81% of GPA variation. The school should definitely use SAT as primary admissions criterion.

items.question_text: A contingency table shows the relationship between gender and preference for a new product. Calculate the marginal probability that a person prefers the product.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates sum of preferences divided by total sample size

synthetic_responses.student_response: Sum preferences / total. If 80 of 200 prefer: P(prefer) = 80/200 = 0.4.
Read from one row/column of contingency table.

items.question_text: If P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4, and A and B are independent, find P(A and B).

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates P(A and B) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12

synthetic_responses.student_response: P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B) = 0.3×0.4 = 0.12 for independent events.
P(A and B) = P(A)+P(B) = 0.7.

items.question_text: A medical test has 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. What is the probability of a false positive? Explain what this means.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies false positive rate as 1 - specificity = 10%, and explains the meaning

synthetic_responses.student_response: False positive rate = 1 - specificity = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10 (10%). 10% of disease-free people test positive.
False positive rate = sensitivity = 95%.

items.question_text: This tree diagram shows the outcomes of a two-stage experiment. Calculate the probability of reaching a specific endpoint.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly multiplies probabilities along the path and shows work

synthetic_responses.student_response: Multiply probabilities along path to endpoint. Path: 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.21 probability.
Just find largest probability in diagram.

items.question_text: A student randomly guesses on a 10-question true/false test. What is the expected number of correct answers?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates expected value as 10 × 0.5 = 5

synthetic_responses.student_response: E(X) = n×p = 10×0.5 = 5 correct answers expected from random guessing.
Expected value is most likely outcome, probably 4, 5, or 6 (not sure which).

items.question_text: Two events A and B are mutually exclusive. If P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.3, find P(A or B) and P(A and B).

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies P(A or B) = 0.5 and P(A and B) = 0

synthetic_responses.student_response: P(A or B) = 0.2+0.3 = 0.5. P(A and B) = 0 (can't both occur).

items.question_text: Explain the difference between permutations and combinations, and when you would use each. Include an example.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Distinguishes based on order importance and provides appropriate examples with calculations

synthetic_responses.student_response: Permutations: order matters (5 people in 5 chairs = 5!). Combinations: order irrelevant (committee selection).
Permutations and combinations are identical.

items.question_text: This probability distribution shows the outcomes of a random variable. Calculate the variance and explain what it represents.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates variance as E(X²) - [E(X)]² and interprets as spread of distribution

synthetic_responses.student_response: Variance = E(X²) - [E(X)]². Standard deviation = √variance. Measures spread around mean.
Variance is just average of all distribution values.

items.question_text: A binomial distribution has n=20 and p=0.4. Find the probability of exactly 8 successes.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly applies binomial formula or uses appropriate calculation method

synthetic_responses.student_response: P(X=8) = 8/20 = 0.4 since 8 successes from 20 trials.

items.question_text: Two random variables have correlation coefficient r = 0.6. Interpret this value and explain what it does and does not tell us.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Describes moderate positive relationship, emphasizes no causation implication, notes unexplained variability

synthetic_responses.student_response: r=0.6: moderate positive relationship. r²=0.36 so 36% variance explained. No causation proven.
r=0.6 means strong relationship and one variable causes the other.

items.question_text: A random sample has mean 45 and standard deviation 8. What sample size would be needed to have a standard error of 1?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly sets up SE = σ/√n and solves for n = 64

synthetic_responses.student_response: SE = σ/√n, so 1 = 8/√n gives √n = 8, n = 64.
Need n = 8 students when SE = 1 and SD = 8.

items.question_text: Explain why the normal distribution is appropriate for modeling sample means even when the population is not normally distributed.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly references Central Limit Theorem and discusses conditions for applicability

synthetic_responses.student_response: Central Limit Theorem: sample means ~normal for large samples (n≥30) regardless of population. Justifies normal-based inference.
Sample means normal because all populations are normal.

items.question_text: A significance test for a population proportion gives p-value = 0.03. What can you conclude at the 0.05 significance level?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly concludes to reject null hypothesis since p < α

synthetic_responses.student_response: p=0.03 < 0.05=α, so reject H₀. Statistically significant evidence against null.
p=0.03 means 3% chance alternative hypothesis is true.

items.question_text: Compare two datasets with the same mean but different correlation structures. How would this affect inference about their relationship?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Discusses how correlation affects predictability and the strength of inferences

synthetic_responses.student_response: Stronger correlation improves predictability and power of inference. Higher correlation narrows confidence intervals and strengthens hypothesis tests.
Correlation doesn't affect inference strength or predictions.

items.question_text: A company has three machines producing widgets. Machine A produces 30% of widgets with 2% defect rate, Machine B produces 50% with 3% defect rate, and Machine C produces 20% with 1% defect rate. If a widget is randomly selected and found to be defective, what is the probability it came from Machine B? Use Bayes' theorem.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies the probability statement and sets up the formula
Correctly calculates P(Machine B | defective) using total probability

synthetic_responses.student_response:
P(B|D) = P(D|B)P(B) / P(D)

P(D) = total probability ≈ 0.023
P(B|D) ≈ 0.65 or 65%

P(B|D) = P(B) × P(D|B) = 0.50 × 0.03 = 0.015 or 1.5%

Machine B is unlikely to be the source of defects.

items.question_text: A survey of 500 high school students asks about their math anxiety level (low, medium, high) and whether they plan to pursue STEM majors (yes/no). A contingency table shows that 80% of low-anxiety students pursue STEM, compared to 40% of high-anxiety students. (a) Construct the complete contingency table from the given information, showing all counts and marginal totals. (b) Is there evidence of an association between anxiety level and STEM pursuit? Perform a chi-square test of independence (α = 0.05) and interpret the results. (c) Calculate appropriate conditional probabilities. What do these probabilities suggest about the relationship between anxiety and STEM pursuit? (d) Interpret your conclusions in context. What limitations might this observational data have for drawing conclusions about this relationship?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly constructs complete table with proper row/column organization, all counts, and marginal totals from given percentages
Calculates chi-square statistic correctly, identifies degrees of freedom, finds p-value, and makes conclusion at α = 0.05
Calculates conditional probabilities (e.g., P(STEM|low anxiety), P(STEM|high anxiety)) and interprets differences meaningfully
Concludes about association in context; discusses limitations (e.g., causation, sampling method, self-report bias, generalizability)

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a) Contingency table:
Low anxiety: 400×0.80 = 320 STEM, 80 not STEM = 400 total
Medium anxiety: Unknown directly, assume similar distribution
High anxiety: 400×0.40 = 160 STEM, 240 not STEM = 400 total
(Adjusting: if 50/25/25 split on anxiety, and given percentages)

            STEM    Not STEM   Total
Low         80      20         100
Med         75      25         100  
High        40      60         100
Total       195     105        300

(b) Chi-square test: Expected values under independence. χ² ≈ 18.5, df=2, p<0.001. Strong evidence of association between anxiety and STEM pursuit.

(c) P(STEM|low) = 0.80, P(STEM|med) = 0.75, P(STEM|high) = 0.40. Conditional probabilities show clear pattern: lower anxiety students are much more likely to pursue STEM.

(d) There is a strong association: high-anxiety students are significantly less likely to pursue STEM (40% vs. 80% for low-anxiety). Limitations: self-report bias, causation unclear (does anxiety cause reduced STEM interest, or does STEM anxiety reduce pursuit?), sample may not generalize to all schools/demographics.

(a) The contingency table would have rows for anxiety level (low/med/high) and columns for STEM yes/no. With 500 students and the given percentages, roughly 320 low-anxiety pursue STEM, 160 high-anxiety pursue STEM.

(b) Chi-square test tests if anxiety and STEM pursuit are independent. The test would likely show they're associated (p<0.05).

(c) Conditional probabilities: P(STEM|low anxiety) = 0.80 is high, P(STEM|high anxiety) = 0.40 is lower, showing anxiety relates to STEM pursuit.

(d) The data suggest anxious students are less likely to pursue STEM. However, we don't know if anxiety causes the reduced pursuit or if other factors are involved.

(a) Contingency table with anxiety levels and STEM pursuit:
            STEM    No STEM
Low         320     80
High        160     240

(b) Chi-square: χ² ≈ 20, p < 0.05, evidence of association.

(c) Conditional probabilities show lower anxiety students more likely to pursue STEM.

(d) Association found; limitations include potential confounders.

(a) Contingency table shows 500 students split by anxiety (80% low, 20% high) and STEM (60% yes, 40% no):
            STEM    No STEM
Low         240     160
High        60      40

(b) χ² ≈ 8.2, df=1, p≈0.004. Significant association between anxiety and STEM pursuit.

(c) P(STEM) = 0.60 overall; P(STEM|low) = 0.60; P(STEM|high) = 0.60. No difference in conditional probabilities.

(d) Despite the chi-square test being significant, the data show no actual difference in STEM pursuit rates by anxiety level, suggesting the association may be due to sample size effects.

items.question_text: A scatterplot shows x values from 10 to 50 and y values that increase as x increases. The relationship appears linear. What is the direction and strength of correlation?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Identifies positive direction and moderate to strong strength based on plot description

synthetic_responses.student_response: Positive direction (y↑ as x↑). Moderately strong based on tight linear pattern with limited scatter.
Linear relationship means correlation is perfect (r=1).

items.question_text: A linear regression model has R² = 0.64. Interpret this value in context.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly explains that 64% of variability in y is explained by x

synthetic_responses.student_response: R²=0.64: 64% of y variability explained by x. Other 36% from other factors/error.
R²=0.64 means x explains 64% of x's variance.

items.question_text: Using this scatter plot with regression line, predict the y-value for a new x-value and explain your method.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Uses equation or visual interpolation to make reasonable prediction and explains limitations

synthetic_responses.student_response: Interpolate along regression line for x-value. Predictions uncertain; only within data range.
Extrapolate beyond data using regression line.

items.question_text: The regression line is y = 3x + 5. What does the slope tell us about the relationship?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly interprets that for each unit increase in x, y increases by 3 units on average

synthetic_responses.student_response: For each 1-unit x increase, y increases 3 units. Slope = rate of change.
Slope=3 means x is much more important than y.

items.question_text: Why should you not use regression to predict y-values far beyond the range of your data?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that relationship may not hold outside observed range (extrapolation bias)

synthetic_responses.student_response: Relationship may not hold beyond observed range. Assumes pattern continues, often false.
Regression line extends infinitely, so predict as far as needed.

items.question_text: A regression analysis shows a significant relationship, but the residual plot reveals a curved pattern. What does this suggest about your model?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies that linear model is inappropriate and suggests non-linear relationship

synthetic_responses.student_response: Curved residuals suggest non-linear relationship. Linear model inappropriate; try quadratic/exponential.
Curved residuals mean model is perfect with smooth curve.

items.question_text: This residual plot shows several outliers. Discuss what outliers might mean and whether to remove them.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Discusses whether outliers are errors vs. real phenomena, effect on regression, and decision rationale

synthetic_responses.student_response: Outliers: errors or real unusual observations. Investigate cause. Removal changes regression. Only remove if confirmed error.
Always remove all outliers to improve fit.

items.question_text: Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the regression slope. What does this interval tell us?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly constructs CI using t-distribution and explains what it means for the relationship

synthetic_responses.student_response: CI = b ± t*(SE_b). If excludes 0, slope significantly different from 0.
Slope CI same as intercept CI.

items.question_text: A study collects data on hours studied (x) and test score (y) for 25 students. Calculate the correlation coefficient and regression equation. Interpret both the slope and intercept.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates correlation using appropriate formula or method
Correctly finds least squares regression line with appropriate intercept and slope
Provides meaningful interpretation of both parameters in context

synthetic_responses.student_response:
r = Σ[(x-x̄)(y-ȳ)] / √[Σ(x-x̄)²Σ(y-ȳ)²]

Assuming data calculations give r ≈ 0.82

Regression line: ŷ = a + bx where b = r(sy/sx)
If sx ≈ 8, sy ≈ 5, then b = 0.82(5/8) ≈ 0.51

ŷ = (ȳ - b×x̄) + 0.51x ≈ 2.5 + 0.51x

Slope interpretation: For each additional hour of study, test score increases by about 0.51 points.
Intercept interpretation: When x=0 (no study), predicted score is 2.5 (not meaningful in context; test likely out of 100).

Correlation r ≈ 0.80, fairly strong positive.

Regression equation approximately: ŷ = 3 + 0.5x

The slope means each hour of study adds about 0.5 points to the test score.

r ≈ 0.8 (positive correlation)
ŷ = a + bx with slope around 0.5

r ≈ 0.75

Regression: ŷ = 5 + 0.75x

The intercept 5 means students who study 0 hours score 5 points on the test. The slope 0.75 means each hour of study adds 0.75 points.

items.question_text: A school collects data on student GPA (y), hours studied per week (x₁), and class attendance rate (x₂). Develop a multiple regression model, interpret coefficients, assess overall model fit, and discuss how multicollinearity might affect your results.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly specifies multiple regression model with proper notation
Interprets each coefficient as partial effect controlling for other variables
Uses R², F-test, or residual analysis to assess fit; discusses limitations
Explains how multicollinearity inflates standard errors and affects interpretation

synthetic_responses.student_response:
ŷ = a + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂

Where y = GPA, x₁ = hours studied/week, x₂ = attendance rate

Example output: ŷ = 1.2 + 0.15x₁ + 1.5x₂

Coefficients interpretation (partial effects, controlling for the other variable):
- b₁ = 0.15: Each additional study hour increases GPA by 0.15 points (holding attendance constant)
- b₂ = 1.5: Each 10% increase in attendance increases GPA by 0.15 points (holding study hours constant)

Model assessment: R² ≈ 0.68 means 68% of GPA variation explained by these two variables. F-test shows overall model is significant (p<0.001). Adjusted R² accounts for number of variables.

Multicollinearity discussion: If study hours and attendance are correlated (students who study also attend more), the coefficient standard errors inflate. This makes it harder to separate the independent effect of each variable. VIF > 5 would indicate problematic multicollinearity. Solution: remove one variable or use regularization techniques.

Multiple regression model: GPA = a + b₁(study hours) + b₂(attendance)

Possible results: GPA = 1.0 + 0.12(hours) + 1.8(attendance)

This means both study hours and attendance positively affect GPA. R² ≈ 0.65 is decent fit. Multicollinearity could be an issue if study and attendance are related.

Model: ŷ = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂

Both variables likely positive effect on GPA. R² tells overall fit. Multicollinearity occurs when predictors are correlated.

ŷ = 0.5 + 0.25(hours) + 2.0(attendance)

Interpretation: For every hour studied, GPA increases by 0.25 regardless of attendance rate. The model explains all GPA variation (R² = 1.0) with these two variables.

Multicollinearity is not a concern because both variables are independently important.

items.question_text: Define statistics and explain the difference between descriptive and inferential statistics.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Defines statistics as science of data analysis; correctly distinguishes descriptive (summarizing data) from inferential (drawing conclusions about populations)

synthetic_responses.student_response: Statistics is the science of collecting, analyzing, and interpreting data. Descriptive statistics summarizes data using tools like means, medians, and standard deviations. Inferential statistics uses sample data to draw conclusions about populations, testing hypotheses and estimating parameters.
Statistics is just calculating averages. Descriptive statistics is when you describe numbers, and inferential statistics is when you make up data about groups.

items.question_text: Classify each variable as categorical or quantitative: (a) student ID number, (b) gender, (c) test score, (d) favorite color.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly classifies: (a) quantitative, (b) categorical, (c) quantitative, (d) categorical

synthetic_responses.student_response: (a) student ID - quantitative (but could be categorical depending on context), (b) gender - categorical, (c) test score - quantitative, (d) favorite color - categorical
(a) quantitative, (b) quantitative, (c) categorical, (d) categorical

items.question_text: A survey asks 500 people about their income. What is the population and what is the sample?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies population as all people (or relevant group) and sample as the 500 surveyed

synthetic_responses.student_response: Population: all people whose income we want to know about. Sample: the 500 people who were surveyed.
Population: the survey. Sample: 500 people.

items.question_text: Calculate the mean of: 12, 15, 18, 21, 24.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates mean as 18

items.question_text: Identify whether each scenario involves a parameter or a statistic: (a) average salary of all employees at a company, (b) average salary from a sample of 100 employees.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies (a) parameter (from population) and (b) statistic (from sample)

synthetic_responses.student_response: (a) parameter - describes the entire population of company employees. (b) statistic - describes only the sample of 100 employees.
(a) statistic, (b) parameter

items.question_text: Explain why random sampling is preferable to convenience sampling for conducting a survey.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that random sampling reduces bias and ensures representativeness, while convenience sampling is subject to selection bias

synthetic_responses.student_response: Random sampling reduces selection bias by giving each person equal chance of selection. Convenience sampling relies on easy-to-reach people, which may not represent the population well.
Random sampling is more random than convenience sampling and produces better data.

items.question_text: Calculate the standard deviation of: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. (Use sample standard deviation.)

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly calculates sample standard deviation as approximately 3.16

synthetic_responses.student_response: Mean = 6, Variance = sum((x-6)^2)/4 = 20/4 = 5, SD = sqrt(5) ≈ 2.24
SD ≈ 3.16 (using formula with n in denominator instead of n-1)

items.question_text: A researcher wants to study the relationship between exercise and heart health. Explain why this would be better studied with an observational study than an experiment.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains ethical or practical constraints on random assignment; discusses how observational study can still provide useful information

synthetic_responses.student_response: It's unethical to randomly assign people to exercise vs. not exercise for 10 years. An observational study can still show relationships and provide useful evidence about the benefits of exercise.
Experiments need random assignment, which is impossible here, so an observational study is the only option.

items.question_text: Create a frequency table for the following data: A, B, A, C, B, A, B, A. Include frequencies and relative frequencies.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Creates correct table with categories (A, B, C), frequencies (4, 3, 1), and relative frequencies (0.5, 0.375, 0.125)

synthetic_responses.student_response:
Category | Frequency | Relative Frequency
A | 4 | 0.5
B | 3 | 0.375
C | 1 | 0.125
A=4, B=3, C=1 (missing relative frequencies)

items.question_text: Explain what it means for a statistic to be an unbiased estimator of a parameter.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that the expected value of the statistic equals the parameter; or that on average across many samples, the statistic centers on the true parameter

synthetic_responses.student_response: An unbiased estimator has an expected value equal to the parameter. On average across many samples, the estimator centers on the true population value.
Unbiased means the estimator is always correct and doesn't have errors.

items.question_text: In a normal distribution with mean 500 and SD 100, what z-score corresponds to the 84th percentile?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies z-score as 1 (approximately; 84th percentile is 1 SD above mean)

synthetic_responses.student_response: z = 1. The 84th percentile is one standard deviation above the mean. Using z-table, z ≈ 1 corresponds to approximately 0.84 cumulative probability.
z ≈ 0.84 (confusing percentile with z-score)

items.question_text: Explain why the standard normal distribution is useful even if a dataset does not follow a normal distribution.

rubric.learner_facing_text: References Central Limit Theorem; explains that sample means are approximately normal; or describes z-score standardization

synthetic_responses.student_response: The Central Limit Theorem states that sample means are approximately normally distributed regardless of the population distribution. This allows us to use normal-based inference even when the raw data aren't normal.
The standard normal distribution works because it's the most common distribution in nature.

items.question_text: A bimodal distribution has two peaks. What does this tell you about the data, and how might it affect summary statistics like the mean?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that bimodality suggests two distinct groups or processes; discusses how mean can be misleading if it falls between the peaks

synthetic_responses.student_response: Bimodality suggests two distinct groups or subpopulations in the data. The mean can be misleading because it falls between the peaks and doesn't represent any actual group. Using median or reporting separately might be better.
Bimodal means there are two modes. The mean is affected but still useful.

items.question_text: In a right-skewed distribution, which is typically larger: the mean or the median? Explain why.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies mean > median in right-skewed data; explains that the long tail pulls the mean upward

synthetic_responses.student_response: Mean > Median in right-skewed data. The long right tail pulls the mean upward, while the median is more resistant to extreme values.
In right-skewed data, mean is bigger because there are more values on the right.

items.question_text: Two datasets have the same mean and median but different standard deviations. What can you infer about their distributions?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that dataset with larger SD has more spread; both distributions are symmetric (same mean/median); shape may differ

synthetic_responses.student_response: Both distributions are symmetric (equal mean/median). The dataset with larger SD has more spread/variability. Both could be normal or other symmetric shapes, but the shapes may differ in other ways.
The dataset with larger SD is more spread out. They might have different shapes.

items.question_text: Analyze this histogram showing test scores. What does the shape tell you about student performance?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Describes shape (normal, skewed, bimodal); interprets center and spread; discusses what shape suggests about student performance

synthetic_responses.student_response: The histogram shows [shape description]. The distribution is approximately [normal/skewed/bimodal], centered around [center value], with [variability description]. This suggests [interpretation about performance].
The histogram shows most scores are in the middle, indicating students did okay on the test.

items.question_text: If you transform a dataset by multiplying all values by 2, how does this affect the mean, median, and standard deviation?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly explains: mean × 2, median × 2, SD × 2; or generally: location multiplied by 2, spread multiplied by 2

synthetic_responses.student_response: Mean × 2, Median × 2, SD × 2. Multiplying all data by a constant multiplies all measures of location and spread by that constant.
The mean stays the same but the SD doubles. The median increases by 2.

items.question_text: A study uses systematic sampling by surveying every 10th person entering a store. What are potential sources of bias?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Identifies that time-of-day effects, non-random entry patterns, or excluding certain groups could create bias

synthetic_responses.student_response: Bias sources: (1) time-of-day effects (morning vs. evening shoppers differ), (2) people entering at regular intervals may not be random, (3) may exclude people entering at different times.
Could be biased if some people enter more often than others.

items.question_text: Design a matched-pairs experiment to test whether a new study technique improves exam scores compared to the current method.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Specifies that same students use both methods; controls for student differences; includes random assignment of method order

synthetic_responses.student_response: Design: Same students use both methods (counterbalanced). Measure improvement with each method. Randomize order (half use new method first, half use old first) to control for learning effects.
Give students the new method and the old method, then compare their exam scores.

items.question_text: Explain the difference between within-subjects and between-subjects experimental designs.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly distinguishes: within-subjects uses same subjects under different conditions; between-subjects uses different groups for each condition

synthetic_responses.student_response: Within-subjects: same participants experience all conditions. Between-subjects: different groups each experience one condition. Within-subjects controls individual differences but risks carryover effects; between-subjects avoids carryover but requires large samples.
Within-subjects uses the same people. Between-subjects uses different people.

items.question_text: A researcher wants to study student performance across three schools. Should stratified or cluster sampling be used? Justify.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Recommends stratified sampling; explains that schools differ meaningfully and stratification ensures each school is represented

synthetic_responses.student_response: Stratified sampling. Schools differ meaningfully in performance. Stratification ensures all schools are represented proportionally, capturing school-level variation better than cluster sampling would.
Stratified sampling is better because it's more random.

items.question_text: Explain why double-blind design is important in medical experiments testing a new drug.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that neither subjects nor experimenters know treatment; prevents placebo effect and experimenter bias

synthetic_responses.student_response: Neither subjects nor experimenters know who gets the drug vs. placebo. This prevents placebo effects (subject expectations) and experimenter bias (different treatment of groups).
Double-blind means the experiment is hidden from everyone so nobody can cheat.

items.question_text: How would you design a study to determine whether texting while driving increases accident risk without putting participants at risk?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Suggests simulation, observational study, or retrospective analysis; explains why direct experiment would be unethical

synthetic_responses.student_response: Use a driving simulator and test reaction times with and without texting. Or analyze crash data from insurance/accident reports comparing texters vs. non-texters. Ethical because no real risk is introduced.
You could ask people how much texting affects their driving without actually testing it.

items.question_text: This diagram shows the structure of a multi-factor experiment. Identify the factors and levels, and explain how the design controls for confounding.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies factors and levels; explains how factorial design allows separation of individual effects

synthetic_responses.student_response: Factors: [list them]. Levels: [for each factor]. The factorial design allows estimation of individual factor effects and interactions, controlling for confounding by varying factors systematically.
This experiment has multiple treatments arranged in a design that controls some things.

items.question_text: Distinguish between selection bias, response bias, and measurement bias. Give an example of each.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly distinguishes three types and provides relevant examples for each

synthetic_responses.student_response: Selection bias: surveying only mall shoppers excludes non-shoppers. Response bias: people uncomfortable discussing finances may refuse. Measurement bias: asking 'How much do you earn?' may get false answers (social desirability).
Selection bias is when you pick wrong people. Response and measurement biases involve getting wrong answers.

items.question_text: Explain the relationship between statistical significance and effect size. Can a result be statistically significant but not practically significant?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that significance (p-value) differs from effect size (magnitude); yes, large sample can produce significant tiny effects

synthetic_responses.student_response: Statistical significance (p-value < α) means evidence against H₀. Effect size measures magnitude of the difference. Yes, large samples can produce significant tiny effects that aren't practically meaningful (e.g., 1% improvement).
Statistical significance and effect size are the same thing - they both tell you if results matter.

items.question_text: What is a Type II error, and how does it relate to statistical power?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Defines Type II error as failing to reject false null; explains power as 1 - P(Type II error)

synthetic_responses.student_response: Type II error: failing to reject H₀ when it's false (false negative). Power = P(reject H₀ | H₀ false) = 1 - P(Type II error) = 1 - β.
Type II error is when you make a mistake. Power is related but I'm not sure how.

items.question_text: Explain why increasing the sample size increases the power of a hypothesis test.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that larger sample reduces standard error, allowing better discrimination between H₀ and H₁

synthetic_responses.student_response: Larger n reduces SE = σ/√n. Smaller SE means the sampling distribution is narrower, so we're better able to distinguish between H₀ and H₁ values.
More data is better, so bigger samples have more power.

items.question_text: Compare frequentist and Bayesian approaches to hypothesis testing. What is a prior, and how does it influence Bayesian inference?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Distinguishes philosophy and method; explains prior as initial belief; discusses how prior combines with data

synthetic_responses.student_response: Frequentist: p-value probability of data given H₀ is true. Bayesian: uses Bayes' theorem to update beliefs. Prior: initial probability distribution over parameter values before seeing data. Prior combines with likelihood to produce posterior.
Bayesian uses a prior, frequentist doesn't. They give different answers.

items.question_text: What is the multiple comparisons problem, and how can it be addressed in statistical analysis?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that repeated tests inflate Type I error; mentions Bonferroni correction, false discovery rate, or pre-registration

synthetic_responses.student_response: Performing many tests at α = 0.05 inflates Type I error. Solution: use Bonferroni correction (α/number of tests), false discovery rate control, or pre-register hypotheses.
If you do many tests, some will be significant by chance even if nothing is real.

items.question_text: Explain when and why you would use a nonparametric test instead of a parametric test. Give an example.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains violations of parametric assumptions (normality, equal variance); gives example like Mann-Whitney U vs. t-test

synthetic_responses.student_response: Use nonparametric tests when: normality violated, variances unequal, or sample too small to check assumptions. Example: Mann-Whitney U (nonparametric) vs. t-test (parametric) for two independent groups with non-normal data.
Nonparametric tests don't assume a distribution, so they're more flexible but less powerful.

items.question_text: Describe how bootstrap methods can be used to estimate confidence intervals without assuming a specific distribution.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains resampling with replacement; distribution-free approach; generating empirical sampling distribution

synthetic_responses.student_response: Bootstrap: resample original data with replacement many times (e.g., 10,000 bootstrap samples). Calculate statistic for each resample (e.g., mean). 95% CI uses 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. No distributional assumptions needed.
Bootstrap is resampling your data to make an empirical distribution and get confidence intervals from it.

items.question_text: What is the curse of dimensionality, and how does it affect statistical analysis with many variables?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains that data becomes sparse in high dimensions; sample size requirements increase exponentially

synthetic_responses.student_response: Curse of dimensionality: as number of variables increases, data becomes sparse (volume grows exponentially). Sample size needed to estimate parameters grows exponentially. Distances between points become meaningless; many algorithms fail.
With many variables, you need a lot more data and things get complicated.

items.question_text: Explain how regularization (like ridge or lasso regression) addresses overfitting in machine learning models.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Explains penalty on large coefficients; prevents models from fitting noise; balances bias-variance trade-off

synthetic_responses.student_response: Regularization (ridge/lasso) adds penalty term to loss function proportional to coefficient size. Shrinks large coefficients, preventing model from fitting noise. Balances model fit vs. complexity (bias-variance trade-off).
Regularization prevents overfitting by making the model simpler.

items.question_text: What is the difference between a confidence interval and a credible interval, and when would you use each?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Distinguishes frequentist confidence intervals from Bayesian credible intervals; notes different interpretations

synthetic_responses.student_response: Confidence interval (frequentist): if we repeated sampling, 95% of intervals would contain true parameter. Credible interval (Bayesian): given observed data and prior, 95% probability true parameter is in interval. Use CI for frequentist framework, credible interval for Bayesian.
They're pretty much the same thing but Bayesian uses a prior.

items.question_text: Explain the difference between observational data and experimental data.

rubric.learner_facing_text: Observational: collected without manipulation; Experimental: involves intervention/random assignment

synthetic_responses.student_response: Observational data: collected without intervention; researcher observes natural variation. Experimental data: researcher manipulates an independent variable and observes effects on dependent variable.
Observational data is when you observe things. Experimental data is when you experiment with things.

items.question_text: A test score distribution has mean 75 and SD 8. What percentage falls between 67 and 83?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Correctly identifies ±1 SD range as approximately 68%

synthetic_responses.student_response: 67 to 83 is 75±8, which is mean ± 1 SD. By empirical rule, approximately 68% of values fall within 1 SD of mean.
It's about half the data, so approximately 50%.

items.question_text: What is the relationship between variance and standard deviation?

rubric.learner_facing_text: SD is square root of variance

synthetic_responses.student_response: Standard deviation is the square root of variance. Variance = SD². If variance is 25, then SD = 5.
Variance and standard deviation measure the same thing, just called different names.

items.question_text: What is the difference between an experiment and a survey?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Experiment manipulates; survey observes

synthetic_responses.student_response: Experiment: researcher manipulates variables and assigns treatments to groups. Survey: researcher asks questions and observes responses without manipulation.
An experiment is when you test something, a survey is when you ask people.

items.question_text: What is random assignment and why is it important in experiments?

rubric.learner_facing_text: Randomly assigns subjects to groups; controls confounding

synthetic_responses.student_response: Random assignment: randomly assigning subjects to treatment groups. It creates comparable groups and controls for confounding variables, allowing causal inference.
Random assignment means picking random people for your study.
